function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to walk you through what you’d normally do, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, inspect its files, or push commits back to GitHub from here. What I can do is give you a concrete example of what each of those artifacts would look like for a typical “nodejs‑welcome” project, and then show you how you could generate the Dockerfile and Kubernetes YAML automatically using the helper functions that were supplied.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re doing this on a CI machine or a fresh VM, make sure you have SSH keys set up so that `git@github.com` works without prompting for a password.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create artefacts

Below is a quick “snapshot” of what a minimal Node.js repo might contain:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `package.json` | Declares dependencies (`express`, etc.) and start script (`npm start`) |
| `app.js` (or `index.js`) | Entry point of the application |
| `.dockerignore` | Excludes `node_modules`, `.git`, etc. from the build context |

### 2.1 Create/Update Dockerfile

If you want me to generate a Dockerfile for you automatically, you can call the helper function like this:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "node app.js"
}
```

When you run that through the `create_a_docker_file` function, it will write a Dockerfile similar to the one below into the `./nodejs-welcome` directory.

#### Sample Dockerfile

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` gives you a small, production‑ready base image.  
> * `npm ci` installs only the exact versions listed in `package-lock.json`.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the port your Express app listens on.  

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML

Similarly, you can generate a deployment + service file with the helper function:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 3,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "LoadBalancer"
}
```

That will produce a `k8s.yaml` (or whatever you choose to name it) in the same directory. Here’s what the output looks like:

#### Sample Kubernetes YAML

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 3 replicas of your container.  
> * Exposes the pod’s port 3000 to the cluster.  
> * Creates a LoadBalancer service that forwards external traffic on port 80 to the pods.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest

      - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
        with:
          manifests: k8s.yaml
          images: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **Key points**  
> * The workflow triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * It builds the Docker image and pushes it to your registry.  
> * It then applies the Kubernetes manifests (you’ll need to store your kubeconfig in a secret).  

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Recap

| Step | Command / Action |
|------|------------------|
| 1 | `git clone ... && cd nodejs-welcome` |
| 2.1 | Call `create_a_docker_file` or hand‑write Dockerfile |
| 2.2 | Call `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` or hand‑write YAML |
| 2.3 | Create `.github/workflows/build.yml` |
| 3 | `git add ...` |
| 4 | `git commit && git push` |

Feel free to copy the sample Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow into your repo, adjust the image names, registry credentials, and secrets accordingly, and then commit/push. Once you push, the workflow will kick off automatically and build/push your image.
